req.title: Consistency in a shopping cart and a bank ledger
req.prompt: A shopping cart service and a bank ledger service both keep running during a network partition between two data centres. For each one, say whether you favour consistency or availability, and explain what the user experiences and why that is acceptable.
tips: Name the failure you are designing for.
Say what the user sees in each case.

rubric.point: Chooses consistency for the bank ledger
Chooses availability for the shopping cart
Mentions the network partition and that a choice is forced
Describes the user-visible consequence (error versus stale data)
Explains how cart conflicts are reconciled later

req.name: First question

req.title: Payments and notifications across a broken link
req.prompt: Two services in different data centres lose their connection for ten minutes: a payments service and a notifications service. Explain what each should do while the link is down, and how you make sure nothing is lost or duplicated afterwards.
tips: Explain your reasoning, not just the names.

rubric.point: Payments avoid guessing and stay correct (refuse or queue as pending)
Notifications keep working (availability first)
Uses idempotency or de-duplication
Reconciles after the link returns
Detects the problem with monitoring or alerts

req.name: Second question

db.title: Choosing stores for a small marketplace
db.prompt: You are building a marketplace with orders and payments, user login sessions, and product search with typo tolerance. Which data stores would you use, and why? Say which one is the source of truth.
tips: One store per job.
Say how the stores stay in sync.

rubric.point: Uses a relational database for orders and payments because of transactions
Uses a key-value store such as Redis for sessions
Uses a search engine for product search
Names a single source of truth and explains how other stores are fed from it
Gives a trade-off or reason rather than just naming products

db.name: First question

db.title: Stores for a fitness app
db.prompt: A fitness app stores workouts, a social feed of friends' activity, and a leaderboard that updates every few seconds. Choose stores and explain how data moves between them.
tips: Explain your reasoning, not just the names.

rubric.point: A durable relational source of truth for workouts
An in-memory store such as Redis sorted sets for the leaderboard
A precomputed or cached feed
Moves data between stores with events, queues or change data capture
Accepts that derived stores can lag

db.name: Second question

datatypes.title: Matching workloads to specialised stores
datatypes.prompt: Pick a data store for each of these and justify it: (1) CPU metrics every 10 seconds, (2) friend-of-friend recommendations, (3) find images that look similar to an uploaded one, (4) billions of sensor writes per day.
tips: Name the access pattern, not just the product.

rubric.point: Time-series database for metrics
Graph database for friend-of-friend queries
Vector database or embeddings for similar images
Wide-column or write-optimised store for sensor writes
Mentions keeping a source of truth or syncing between stores

datatypes.name: First question

datatypes.title: Stores for a smart city
datatypes.prompt: A smart-city project collects traffic-camera images, bus GPS positions every second, citizen complaints as free text, and a map of roads. Choose a store for each and justify it.
tips: Explain your reasoning, not just the names.

rubric.point: A time-series or wide-column store for GPS positions
Object storage for images
A search engine for free-text complaints
A graph or spatial store for the road map
Keeps metadata or references in a database

datatypes.name: Second question

cap.title: Explain CAP with a real database
cap.prompt: Pick a real database you know. Using the CAP theorem, explain what it does during a network partition, and give an example of a system that makes the opposite choice.
tips: Be concrete: what happens to reads and writes?

rubric.point: States that during a partition you must choose between consistency and availability
Names a consistent (CP) system such as etcd, ZooKeeper, HBase or MongoDB
Names an available (AP) system such as Cassandra or DynamoDB
Describes the concrete behaviour: refuses writes, or serves stale or conflicting data
Mentions tunable consistency, quorums or PACELC

cap.name: First question

cap.title: The last item in two regions
cap.prompt: Your shopping site runs in two regions. During a network split between them, a customer in each region tries to buy the very last item. Explain the options and pick one.
tips: Explain your reasoning, not just the names.

rubric.point: Names the risk of selling it twice
Describes a consistent option (single leader, quorum or refusing one sale)
Describes an available option and how to fix it later (apologise, back-order, compensate)
Connects the choice to partitions and CAP
Justifies the choice with a business cost

cap.name: Second question

apistyles.title: REST, GraphQL or gRPC
apistyles.prompt: Your company has a public partner API, a mobile app with varied screens, and many internal microservices. Choose REST, GraphQL or gRPC for each, and give the main trade-off of your choice.
tips: Think about who the caller is.

rubric.point: REST for the public partner API
GraphQL for the mobile app to avoid over-fetching
gRPC for internal service-to-service calls
Mentions caching, simplicity or tooling as a reason for REST
Mentions a downside such as GraphQL query cost or gRPC browser support

apistyles.name: First question

apistyles.title: APIs for a delivery company
apistyles.prompt: A food delivery company has a driver app that needs live location updates, a restaurant dashboard that shows orders with many details, and a public API for partners. Choose API styles and justify each.
tips: Explain your reasoning, not just the names.

rubric.point: Streaming for live driver location (WebSocket, gRPC streaming or server-sent events)
GraphQL for the detail-heavy dashboard
REST for the public partner API
Plans for versioning and backward compatibility
Protects the API with authentication and rate limits

apistyles.name: Second question

solid.title: Refactor a God class
solid.prompt: An OrderService class validates orders, saves them to MySQL, sends confirmation emails, and has a long if/else chain for discount types. Describe how you would refactor it using SOLID principles, and what you would not over-engineer.
tips: Name the principle behind each change.

rubric.point: Splits responsibilities (validation, persistence, notification)
Replaces the if/else with strategies or polymorphism (open/closed)
Depends on abstractions and injects them
Mentions testability
Warns against over-engineering or needless abstraction

solid.name: First question

solid.title: Redesign a notification service
solid.prompt: You have a NotificationService with sendEmail, sendSms and sendPush and a growing if/else on channel. You will soon need WhatsApp, and you want to test the service without sending real messages. How do you redesign it?
tips: Explain your reasoning, not just the names.

rubric.point: One interface with a class per channel (strategy)
Adds WhatsApp without editing existing code (open/closed)
Injects the channel so tests can use a fake
Separates formatting from sending (single responsibility)
Avoids over-engineering

solid.name: Second question

oop.title: Model a parking lot
oop.prompt: Design the classes for a parking lot. List the entities, how they relate, and the key methods. Mention one concurrency concern.
tips: Nouns become classes, verbs become methods.

rubric.point: Identifies the core entities (Vehicle, Spot, Ticket, ParkingLot or Level)
Describes relationships such as has-a, composition or is-a
Lists key methods such as park, unpark and calculate fee
Uses a pricing or allocation strategy rather than hard-coding
Raises concurrent allocation of the same spot and a fix (lock or atomic update)

oop.name: First question

oop.title: Design an elevator system
oop.prompt: Design the classes for an elevator system in a building with several elevators. Cover the entities, how a request is assigned to an elevator, and one tricky edge case.
tips: Explain your reasoning, not just the names.

rubric.point: Identifies the entities (Elevator, Request, Floor, Controller)
Models elevator states (idle, moving up, moving down)
Uses an assignment strategy (nearest, scheduling)
Handles concurrent requests with a queue or locking
Names a tricky edge case (overload, emergency stop, door)

oop.name: Second question

patterns.title: Pick a pattern for a vending machine
patterns.prompt: A vending machine behaves differently when it is idle, holding money, dispensing, or out of stock. Which design pattern would you use? Sketch the classes and say why an if/else chain is worse.
tips: Name the pattern and its parts.

rubric.point: Identifies the State pattern
Defines a state interface with concrete states
Has a context class that delegates to the current state
Describes state transitions
Explains why if/else chains get hard to maintain

patterns.name: First question

patterns.title: Undo and plugins in an editor
patterns.prompt: A text editor needs undo and redo, and also lets users add many kinds of toolbar buttons from plugins. Which design patterns would you use and how?
tips: Explain your reasoning, not just the names.

rubric.point: Command pattern for undoable actions
Undo and redo stacks for history
A plugin interface, factory or registry for toolbar buttons
Observer to keep the user interface updated
Mentions a trade-off such as memory or complexity

patterns.name: Second question

interview.title: Start a URL shortener design
interview.prompt: You are asked to design a URL shortener. Describe the first steps you take before drawing any boxes.
tips: What do you ask? What do you calculate?

rubric.point: Clarifies requirements and scope
Asks about scale such as users, requests per second or links per day
Estimates traffic or storage
Notes the read-heavy ratio
Mentions defining the API or data model before the design

interview.name: First question

interview.title: Open a ride-hailing design
interview.prompt: You are asked to design a ride-hailing service like Uber. List the clarifying questions you would ask and the main components you would sketch first.
tips: Explain your reasoning, not just the names.

rubric.point: Asks clarifying questions about scope and requirements
Handles live location with GPS, WebSockets or geospatial indexing
Includes a matching or dispatch service
Includes payments and pricing
Estimates scale (users, drivers, requests per second)

interview.name: Second question

mvp.title: Scope a first release
mvp.prompt: You have one engineer and no users yet. List what you will build first and what you will deliberately leave out, with reasons.
tips: Think about the one loop that proves the idea.

rubric.point: Builds the single core user loop first
Chooses a simple stack such as a monolith and one database
Leaves out Kubernetes, microservices or multi-region
Keeps cheap essentials like backups, logging or basic security
Plans to learn from real users early

mvp.name: First question

mvp.title: Scope a delivery marketplace
mvp.prompt: A founder wants to launch a food-delivery marketplace in one city with a team of three. What do you build first, what do you buy instead of building, and what do you postpone?
tips: Explain your reasoning, not just the names.

rubric.point: Builds the core order-to-delivery loop for one city first
Buys instead of builds (payments, maps, notifications)
Postpones custom routing, microservices or other heavy parts
Runs some steps manually at first
Measures with real users

mvp.name: Second question

search.title: Design search for an online shop
search.name: First question
search.prompt: An online shop has 20 million products. Design its search box with typo-tolerant results and suggestions while the user types. Say what you store, how a query is answered quickly, how the index stays up to date and how suggestions work.
tips: Say what the index is made of.
Say how it stays in sync with the database.

rubric.point: Uses an inverted index (word to documents) rather than scanning the database
Explains analysis of text (tokenising, lowercasing, stemming) and using it for both documents and queries
Explains ranking, for example BM25 or TF-IDF plus business signals
Keeps the index in sync from the database through a queue or change feed and accepts a small lag
Designs suggestions with a trie, n-grams or precomputed popular prefixes, with caching or debouncing

geo.title: Design 'find nearby drivers'
geo.name: First question
geo.prompt: A ride app has one million drivers online, each sending a position every few seconds. Design the service that returns the closest available drivers to a rider. Explain how you index locations, how you store the live positions and how you scale it.
tips: Say how you avoid scanning every driver.
Say what happens at the border of a cell.

rubric.point: Divides the map into cells (geohash, quadtree, H3 or S2) so a search reads only a few cells
Searches neighbouring cells too, because the nearest driver may be across a border
Keeps live positions in memory (for example Redis), not in a disk database
Expires stale positions with a time to live or heartbeat
Partitions by area or city and handles hot dense cells

notify.title: Design a notification system
notify.name: First question
notify.prompt: Design a system that sends push, SMS and email notifications for an app with 50 million users. It must send urgent one-time codes within seconds, run a campaign to all users, and never send the same message twice. Explain the components, the queues, retries and how you prevent duplicates.
tips: Separate urgent from bulk.
Say what a retry does to duplicates.

rubric.point: Uses a queue between the event and the senders, with workers per channel
Hands delivery to providers such as APNs, FCM, Twilio or SES
Separates urgent messages from bulk campaigns using separate queues or priorities
Retries with backoff, and prevents duplicates with an idempotency key
Checks user preferences and rate limits, and processes bounces or unsubscribes

dr.title: Plan disaster recovery for a payment service
dr.name: First question
dr.prompt: A payment service runs in one cloud region. Leadership wants it to survive the loss of that whole region. Explain how you would choose the recovery objectives, what architecture you would pick, how data reaches the second region and how you would prove it works.
tips: Name RPO and RTO.
Say how you will test it.

rubric.point: Defines RPO and RTO and links them to business cost
Chooses a strategy (pilot light, warm standby or active-active) and justifies it
Replicates data to the second region and discusses sync versus async and the resulting lag
Covers failover steps such as health checks, promoting the database and moving traffic with DNS or a global load balancer
Tests the plan with restore tests or game days and keeps a runbook
